planting.note: Set bulbs 2-3 inches deep in spring in well-drained garden soil in full sun to part shade, where a soaking rain or deep watering after a dry spell will trigger bloom.

directions: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun to light part shade; primrose rain lily is a Gulf-region native prized for its narrow-petaled, pale sulfur-yellow flowers with a faint rosy blush on the outer petals, a softer contrast to the more saturated gold of Zephyranthes citrina. Dark green, grass-like foliage persists through most of the warm season and stays dormant during dry stretches, then the plant sends up flower stalks within days of a soaking rain, each bloom lasting about two days before fading. It tolerates both wet and quite dry soils once established and multiplies gradually by offsets to form a tidy, long-lived clump ideal for rock gardens, border edges, and small containers. Leave clumps undisturbed for several years and divide only when flowering thins from crowding.

planting.note: Set bulbs 2-3 inches deep in spring in well-drained garden soil in full sun to part sun, where summer rain events will trigger repeated flushes of bloom.

directions: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to part sun; 'Grandjax' is a multi-generational hybrid (Zephyranthes grandiflora crossed with Z. 'Ajax') bred by Ray Flagg and prized as one of the most floriferous rain lily selections available, opening large, creamy-pink flowers with a white starred throat. Being sterile, it channels all its energy into offsets rather than seed, forming a dense, fast-multiplying clump that can throw dozens to hundreds of blooms in a single flush after a summer downpour or deep watering. It repeats this cycle from summer through early fall and, once established, needs no deadheading or special care beyond well-drained soil. Divide congested clumps in early spring to maintain vigorous flowering and share offsets, since it will not come true or spread from seed.

planting.note: Set bulbs 3-4 inches deep in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, where a late-summer dry spell followed by rain will trigger bloom.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; this Uruguay and Argentina native is distinguished by its notably thin, wire-like foliage and solitary or paired, clear pink, funnel-shaped flowers held at the characteristic upward-tilted Habranthus angle. In its native range it stays dormant through a late-summer dry spell and then blooms in a rapid flush in late summer or early fall once seasonal rains return, a rhythm it repeats reliably in cultivation after a heavy watering. Clumps build slowly by bulb offsets and are best left undisturbed for several seasons in a raised bed, rock garden, or container. Where winters bring more than light, brief frost, grow it in a pot or lift and store bulbs to protect it from prolonged freezing.
